misreading.wrong: Ratzinger's "deeper unity" means monotheism, polytheism, and atheism are finally equivalent — dig deep enough and everything becomes one.
misreading.right: All three confess the unity of the absolute, but they differ decisively over how man deals with it; decisions remain serious.
misreading.quote: a unity that of course cannot be synonymous with identity

argument.tension: Three rival formulas — one God, many gods, no God — yet all three affirm the absolute's unity.
argument.move: Grant the shared conviction, deny identity, and relocate the difference: how man must deal with the absolute, or it with him.
argument.payoff: Atheism becomes a form of the God-question, yet no difference is flattened; both poverty and fullness still point Godward.

rubric: Unity of the absolute shared by all three
Difference lies in dealing with it
Poverty and fullness both point to God

misreading.wrong: Saying "one God" is just arithmetic: monotheism means accepting that the gods number one, a single opinion among others.
misreading.right: It is an existential renunciation of deified bread, love, and power — a declaration of war on every absolutized political claim.
misreading.quote: it is not the registration of one view alongside others but an existential decision

argument.tension: Israel's "Yahweh is an only God" versus the surrounding worship of bread, love, and power — number against decision.
argument.move: Read the Shema as renunciation: the one God unmakes the gods of hunger, Eros, and domination, refusing every god of one's own.
argument.payoff: The first creed line shatters every political claim to totality and protects freedom by relativizing the collective before God.

rubric: Renunciation of bread, love, power idols
Existential decision, not registered opinion
Relativizes all political power absolutely

misreading.wrong: "I am who I am" defines God's essence: God is simply the supreme being, a thing whose nature the name states.
misreading.right: The name is self-revelation in relation, not definition; the Greek "he that is" marries faith to ontology but risks concept replacing name.

argument.tension: The God who names himself, addressable as an individual, versus Platonic Being — unnamed, unnameable, grasped only by concept.
argument.move: Accept the translators' bridge to ontology, then read Exodus against it: only a God who names himself can be invoked.
argument.payoff: Faith and philosophy are wedded without collapse: the name survives the concept because relation outruns definition.

rubric: Greek translation joins faith and ontology
Risk: name replaced by concept
Only self-named God is invocable

misreading.wrong: The patriarchs took over the surrounding El-cult: their God was the highest local deity, attached to holy places like other gods.
misreading.right: They chose El as numen personale: God met on the I–You plane, bound to no place, the God of promise.
misreading.quote: He is not the god of a place but the god of men: the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

argument.tension: The numen locale confines the divine to holy spots and multiplies it; the God of the fathers is personal and boundless.
argument.move: Contrast numen personale with numen locale, then read the plural Elohim as hint that God transcends singular and plural.
argument.payoff: Relation replaces location: Israel's God is the God of all, of hope and irreversible promise — a faint pointer to Trinity.

rubric: Numen personale, not numen locale
Relation on I–You plane, not place
Elohim's plural hints beyond number

misreading.wrong: "I am who I am" states God's essence in itself: it answers Moses' question with a definition of what God is.
misreading.right: It works as rebuff and promise at once: the name dissolves into mystery yet says "I am here for you" — Being-for.
misreading.quote: his Being is expounded, not as Being in itself

argument.tension: The answer looks like a refusal to name God, matching Judges 13 and Genesis 32 — yet Moses gets an answer.
argument.move: Hold both halves: negative theology cancels the name into mystery, while "I am" promises presence — then follow "I am" to Christ.
argument.payoff: Deutero-Isaiah's "I am" becomes John's Christology: Jesus himself is God's name, permanently invocable among us.

rubric: Rebuff: name dissolved into mystery
Promise: "I am here for you"
John: Christ is God's very name

misreading.wrong: God's name reveals his inner nature the way a definition states a thing's essence to a detached observer.
misreading.right: A concept grasps nature in itself; a name makes God invocable. Self-naming is self-giving — handing himself over into coexistence with us.
misreading.quote: he is not so much expressing his inner nature as making himself nameable

argument.tension: The concept asks what a thing is apart from me; the name makes the other invocable, entering relation with me.
argument.move: Contrast concept and name, then show God's self-naming reaches its goal when the name becomes a person in Christ.
argument.payoff: Theology becomes invocation: the goal of the name is not information but callability — God permanently "there" for us.

rubric: Concept seeks essence; name establishes relation
Self-naming is self-giving, not defining
Fulfilled when the name becomes person

misreading.wrong: Readers must choose: the near, personal God of the Bible, or the philosophers' remote infinite Being — the two sides conflict.
misreading.right: Biblical faith holds both sides together: the hidden One is the near One; proximity is the free gift of timeless power.
misreading.quote: only what is hidden is accepted as the One who is near

argument.tension: Personal, invocable self-bestowal versus timeless Being above space and bound to nothing — intimacy and infinity in one God.
argument.move: Refuse to split them: accept Being as person and person as Being itself — the conjunction, not either pole, is the faith.
argument.payoff: No god of one's own: Israel's God is the God of all, and possessing God means universal belonging.

rubric: Nearness: personal, invocable, self-bestowing
Transcendence: Being beyond space and time
Conjunction is the paradox, not choice

misreading.wrong: The early Church betrayed the Bible by choosing Greek philosophy; authentic faith means leaving logos aside for pure piety and revelation.
misreading.right: It continued the Bible's own movement: opting for logos over myth, truth over custom, purified faith from the gods and their deceit.
misreading.quote: carried out its purification by deciding for the God of the philosophers and against the gods

argument.tension: The God of faith versus the God of the philosophers: did the Church sell Moses for Plato — or finish Moses' trajectory?
argument.move: Show the Bible itself already strove toward Being; the Church's decision took that thread and demythologized world and religion definitively.
argument.payoff: Reason and faith stay wedded; Christianity sides with truth against custom, escaping antiquity's collapse into beautiful but empty rite.

rubric: Continues Bible's striving toward Being
Logos over myth, truth over custom
Fideism would repeat antiquity's collapse

misreading.wrong: A God with a heart who seeks and rejoices is naive anthropomorphism; true divinity is the philosophers' remote, unfeeling Being.
misreading.right: The philosophers' God is transformed, not discarded: absolute thought proves to be creative love — a heart is no imperfection.
misreading.quote: Absolute thought is a kind of love; it is not unfeeling idea, but creative, because it is love.

argument.tension: Pure thought circling in self-enclosed eternity versus the biblical God who seeks, waits, rejoices — geometry versus a heart.
argument.move: Identify faith's God with the philosophers', then transform the identification: thought turns out to be love, autarchy turns out to be relation.
argument.payoff: Philosophy is transcended at two points — relation and love — yet its discovery stands: the ground of being is agape.

rubric: Philosophers' God transformed, not abandoned
Absolute thought is really creative love
Relationship transcends self-enclosed autarchy

misreading.wrong: Almighty means omnipotence as irresistible force: God's lordship is proved by controlling every event and crushing all resistance.
misreading.right: The Creed joins "Father" to "Almighty": true almightiness appears only in crib and Cross, where God renounces power and wins through love.
misreading.quote: only becomes clear from a Christian point of view in the crib and the Cross

argument.tension: Father names intimate family love; Almighty names cosmic lordship — Pantokrator's absolute power versus absolute proximity in one description.
argument.move: Harness the first article to the second: let Son and Cross define what almightiness means, reversing maximum and minimum.
argument.payoff: A new concept of power is born: strength as willingness to renounce all power, love stronger than violence.

rubric: Father and Almighty join love and power
Almightiness defined only from crib and Cross
Power perfected as renunciation of force

misreading.wrong: Creation is a one-time fabrication: God crafted the world like a long-dead craftsman, then left it to run by itself.
misreading.right: Creation is being-thought released into freedom by creative freedom: the model is creative mind, and freedom is being's structure.
misreading.quote: the model from which creation must be understood is not the craftsman but the creative mind

argument.tension: Materialism makes meaning a chance by-product of matter; idealism dissolves things into one consciousness — neither yields free, real beings.
argument.move: Concede to idealism that all being is being-thought, then outbid it: things are released into their own independent freedom.
argument.payoff: Logos — idea, freedom, love — stands at the beginning; Christianity becomes a philosophy of freedom, not monism.

rubric: Logos: idea, freedom, love first
Being is being-thought set free
Creation model is creative mind

misreading.wrong: Calling God "personal" is anthropomorphic: the ground of being must be impersonal necessity or anonymous thought, not freedom and love.
misreading.right: A personal logos puts freedom, not necessity, at the ground of being; the particular is supreme, so plurality has its own right.
misreading.quote: the supreme factor in the world is not cosmic necessity but freedom

argument.tension: Anonymous universal consciousness versus personal creative love — necessity versus freedom, the universal versus the irreducible particular.
argument.move: Take "person" seriously: thinking that knows and loves gives its thought freedom; hence particularity and freedom are primordial, not derived.
argument.payoff: Personhood without relation becomes unthinkable: oneness is not the final word, and monotheism's logic leads on to Trinity.

rubric: Personal logos: freedom, love ground being
Primacy of particular over universal
Plurality's own right leads to Trinity

misreading.wrong: The Trinity means three divine personalities cooperating — or three masks God wears, roles played for our benefit in history.
misreading.right: Trinity arose from historical encounter with Father, Son, and Spirit: the threeness is real — God is as he shows himself.
misreading.quote: God is as he shows himself; God does not show himself in a way in which he is not.

argument.tension: God's threeness in encounter versus his oneness in himself: historical masks, or the reality of God's own life?
argument.move: Block both escapes — Subordinationism's minister-God, Monarchianism's masked roles — and remain with the mystery as negative theology.
argument.payoff: Worship and prayer are grounded: we meet God himself, and dogma stands as a frontier notice, not a definition.

rubric: Trinity from encounter, not speculation
God is as he shows himself
Subordinationism and Monarchianism destroy whole

misreading.wrong: Three Persons must mean three divine subjects — three gods loosely united — or else relations merely tacked onto a solitary substance.
misreading.right: Relation is as primordial as substance: the Persons are pure relatedness of word and love, and pure relation is purest unity.
misreading.quote: Person is the pure relation of being related, nothing else.

argument.tension: Divine plurality versus divine unity: threeness must not multiply substances, yet oneness must not erase real relation and dialogue.
argument.move: Locate threeness in relation, not substance: dialogue, word, and love stand beside substance as equally primordial modes of being.
argument.payoff: Pure relation is purest unity — love's multi-unity surpasses the atom — and Christian existence becomes being "from" and "for".

rubric: Threeness in relation, oneness in substance
Relation primordial, not an accident
Pure relation is purest unity, love
